subject: Objection to silencing of public comment at public hearings
comment:
To: St. George City Commission, Council and Mayor -- 5/4/2023

I object to the silencing of the people of St. George city residents by forbidding them speaking at public hearings.

We the people have a right to free speech and redress from our local government officials.

Each elected officer in State, local & municipal positions take an Oath of Office. In this oath, each person swears to support, obey and defend the Constitution of the United States and the constitution of the State of Utah.

The 1st Amendment of the U.S. Constitution protects the right of free speech of the people.

The Utah Constitution Article 1, Section 1 also protects the free speech of the people. "All persons have the inherent and inalienable right to ... assemble peaceably, protest against wrongs, and petition for redress of grievances; to communicate freely their thoughts and opinions...".

On the website of The Utah Division of Archives and Records Service it explains about the Oath of Office. It states "§ Acts of Officials not Voided. No official act of any municipal officer shall be invalid for the reason that he failed to take the oath of office".

I would like to reference the Supreme Court Case Miranda v. Arizona, 384 U.S. 436, 491 "Where rights secured by the Constitution are involved, there can be no rule making or legislation which would abrogate them".

This is an official record of my objection of the City Council and the Mayor of St. George City refusing to allow public comment during public hearings.

Kristen Hafen

subject: Citizen input for CC meeting 05/04/23
comment:
I see no advantage for St. George citizens with this e-bus proposal. The following are my concerns regarding electric vehicles (EVs) and the push to electrify everything:

1. EVs are heavily subsidized by taxpayers and would not be viable in the marketplace without those subsidies.
2. The electric grid is already strained and cannot reliably support large-scale EV adoption, especially in the heat of southern Utah summers.
3. The batteries require mining of rare-earth minerals, much of it done overseas under poor environmental and labor conditions.
4. EV batteries are expensive to replace and difficult to recycle, creating a future disposal problem.
5. The range of electric buses is limited, and performance degrades in extreme temperatures.
6. The up-front and maintenance costs of electric buses exceed those of conventional vehicles.
7. The claimed climate/emissions benefits are overstated once the full life cycle (manufacturing, electricity generation, disposal) is considered.
8. Charging infrastructure is costly and would be funded by taxpayers.
9. This is a top-down agenda being pushed onto the city that does not reflect the actual needs or wishes of St. George citizens.

Please rethink any use of Electric vehicles, appliances, landscaping tools, etc. in the city. Thank you.

subject: Public Comment
comment:
I was shocked when the declaration of NO public comments at the first council meeting of the month was announced. Public comment is a vital part of representative government and should not be eliminated or curtailed. I propose the following rules for a public comment policy:

1. Public comment should be allowed at every regular council meeting.
2. No advance sign-up should be required to speak.
3. Each speaker should be allowed at least three minutes.
4. Comments should be allowed before any vote is taken on an agenda item.
5. The council should not limit the number of speakers.
6. Speakers should be treated with respect and not interrupted.
7. The council should respond to or follow up on substantive concerns raised.
8. The policy should be published and applied consistently.

Thank you for considering these suggestions.

Rich F

comment: Esteemed council people, I am hoping that some monitoring and preventative measures will be provided in regard to traffic safety concerns caused by the upcoming St. George Temple Open House, specifically on 200 E. The Open House is currently planned from September 15th through November 11th, 2023, spanning almost two full months. I live right behind the temple and have to pass it any time I leave my house. It has been a four-year struggle of dodging distracted, rubber necking drivers who pull on and off the road while ogling the building's construction. I have personally almost been hit several times by drivers who are focused on finding the best view to peep through the fence from their vehicle, often driving at a snail's pace speed or driving down the "suicide" lane or the shoulders of the road and swerving back into the normal traffic lane without warning. The apartments in this area are often home to multiple people in one house, such as my household of four active young adults. We rely on the street space for parking, not just for our guests but our own families. The traffic on the road from visitors and construction crews has crowded up the street 5-6 days a week. I can only imagine that once the oldest LDS temple in the world is reopened for public viewing, that the traffic down this street will be impossible to battle. I hope that with the concerns that have come up with other nearby events causing parking and traffic congestion (e.g., the Farmers Market at the nearby Vernon Worthen Park most Saturdays, which I love and frequently attend), that consideration would be taken for an ongoing event such as the Open House. As it is now, the Farmer's Market traffic does not hold a candle to the constant safety issues I have experienced on the roads directly surrounding the temple, especially 200 E. Thank you for all you do for our city. Working in administration for a smaller scale community (SunRiver), I know that the work required to better our community, meet the needs of the constituents, and create functional and fair processes can sometimes feel like figuring out an incomplete algebra equation. Thanks for keeping the world turning around these parts.

subject: City Council-Note Item 6 "Consider approval of Resolution No. 2024-030R approving the City to be a co-signer of the State of Utah's Public Lands Amicus Brief."
comment:
Dear St George City Council,

We are writing in response to last night's agenda item 6 ("Consider approval of Resolution No. 2024-030R approving the City to be a co-signer of the State of Utah's Public Lands Amicus Brief.") as residents of the City of Saint George and members of Conserve Southwest Utah.

Conserve Southwest Utah is strongly opposed to Utah's lawsuit challenging the federal government's control over federal public lands in the state. Washington County's water resources, wildlife habitats, scenic vistas, active communities, and tourism, recreation and real estate economies thrive because of federal public lands. Keeping local lands under federal protection is the best way to ensure long-term, enduring protections for the special places that mean so much to St. George residents.

Conserve Southwest Utah is a local nonprofit with supporters in the City of St. George whose mission is to conserve and steward our area's natural and cultural resources and advocate for Smart Growth policies that enable conservation for the benefit of present and future generations.

Thank you for your consideration of our comments on this issue.

Respectfully,

Judith Rognli, M.A.
City of St. George Resident
Desert Livability Program Manager, Conserve Southwest Utah

Susan Crook, ASLA, PLA
City of St. George Resident
Historical Landscape Architect
Member, Conserve Southwest Utah

subject: Comments on December 5th St. George City Council Meeting
comment:
Dear St. George City Council,

As a Washington County non-profit who has worked for the last two decades to protect our area's beloved public lands and advocate for smart growth, we were disappointed that last night's City Council presentation focused on promoting the proposed Northern Corridor Highway instead of using this time to explore the many, viable options to pursue permanent protections for the Greater Moe's Valley Area.

We respectfully ask that you work with local stakeholders, including Conserve Southwest Utah, to pursue permanent protections to the beloved Greater Moe's Valley Area—a place with important recreational, cultural, and natural resources. And we ask that you use every tool in your toolbox to motivate SITLA to slow down their development of this area.

Last night's City Council's presentation on the Northern Corridor Highway and the Red Hills Parkway Expressway criticized the design of the Red Hills Parkway Expressway, but failed to mention that the traffic studies were conducted by the Dixie MPO's own traffic consultant, Horrocks, not the Bureau of Land Management.

In addition, the presentation failed to acknowledge that:
- Not only was the proposed Northern Corridor Highway not promised, but also our community was promised a future where the open space, recreation, and natural and cultural resources within the Red Cliffs Desert Reserve and National Conservation Area would be protected for the benefit of our community and future generations.
- The proposed Northern Corridor Highway would violate five bedrock environmental laws.
- The design of the Red Hills Parkway Expressway is less than 10% complete, so many specific details would still need to be worked out in conjunction with key community stakeholders.
- A 'no built' and a 'no action' alternative are not the same. Washington County has many tools in its toolbox, especially land-use planning, that would be more effective at alleviating traffic. All of these tools should be explored.
- If the proposed Northern Corridor Highway were approved, a new interchange would be constructed about one mile north of the historic Dixie Sugarloaf.

Most importantly, you do not acknowledge that at least $200 million dollars of taxpayer money (plus ongoing maintenance cost) and resources would be wasted on this highway that does not provide a solution to traffic problems. Time and again, communities have tried this and failed. Provo, Salt Lake, Tucson, Colorado Springs, Boise, and many more cities have tried their best to alleviate congestion through road construction and have seen large increases of congestion regardless. Traffic congestion is not caused by lack of roads, it is caused by prioritizing cars over people in urban planning.

This moment is a crossroad and an opportunity. It is not too late to drop the expensive liability of the proposed Northern Corridor Highway and come together to find approaches towards land-use and transportation planning that truly help us move forward.

Thank you for considering our perspectives.

Respectfully,
Holly Snow Canada (she/her)
Executive Director
Conserve Southwest Utah

subject: Mohave Crossing - Approve Medical/Professional & Retail Space - Disapprove Hotel
comment:
Dear Mayor Randall:

We are writing to express our support for the proposed medical/professional office space and the retail space at the Mohave Crossing development. However, we strongly oppose the plan to build a hotel (one of the three-tiers of the Mojave Crossing Development Project), slated to be built on the lot next to SunRiver (between Sand Piper Dr. and Pioneer Dr., and adjacent to Nighthawk Dr.).

Issue 1. Wrong Location for a Hotel or any 24/7 Operation - We moved to SunRiver three years ago from North Carolina (Air Force Retirees) and have been very happy here. This was our 20th move, and we don't intend to move again. We've lived in many places around the country - nowhere has there been a hotel or any other 24/7 operation so close to a residential development. Hotels have been documented to correlate with increased crime rates (i.e., burglary, theft, assault, drugs, human trafficking, and homicide) in the surrounding areas. Placing such a facility in close proximity to SunRiver's 55+ Retirement Community would seriously jeopardize the safety and security of our community's residents. The proximity of the hotel to our 55+ aged community homes is too close despite the revised site plan for the lot in question. This is not a location for a hotel or any other 24/7 operation no matter how much of an offset is built-in with sidewalks, streets, and landscaping. The transient nature of the business brings people to the area that have no investment in the community and are just too close to vulnerable aged individuals. The appropriate location for a hotel is on the east side of Pioneer Road, sufficiently removed from the residential homes.

Issue 2. Safety and Noise - Building a hotel or other 24/7 operation in our location would disrupt the peaceful living that drew us to SunRiver. The 24/7 operational hours of the hotel and constant influx of guests will exacerbate noise and safety concerns and significantly disturb the peace and tranquility that attracted many of the residents to SunRiver. It will have a definite negative effect on property values and result in decreased property tax revenues from the SunRiver community. We agree with the recommendation that trash collection for anything developed on this lot be limited to the hours of 8:00 am-6:00 pm - no overnight or early morning collection for businesses.

Issue 3. Parking and Traffic - The revised site design for the development does not provide sufficient parking and will result in overflow parking on Sand Piper Drive, which borders residential backyards, creating significant safety and privacy concerns. The design does not accommodate RVs, trailers or large trucks that require a wide turning radius. Consequently, these large vehicles will end up being parked on Sand Piper Drive, immediately adjacent to the SunRiver residences. The design uses shared parking between businesses and only factors in two employee parking spaces for the hotel. This is insufficient - we know from experience that the Hampton Inn & Suites has up to 30 employees onsite during peak times. Hotel employees will also end up being parked on Sand Piper Drive. We strongly recommend that the traffic out of this development be directed to a right-turn-only exit onto Nighthawk Drive, directing traffic away from the SunRiver residences.

We urge the St. George City Council to modify the proposed Mohave Crossing development by doing the following:
1. Disapprove the construction of a hotel or any other 24/7 operation on this site
2. Approve the construction of medical/professional space and retail space with recommended traffic and parking accommodations.

We understand that the property's zoning laws allow a hotel to be built here. However, we firmly believe a hotel is completely inappropriate for this SunRiver neighborhood. It is crucial that the St. George City Council understand the depth of the SunRiver community opposition to building this hotel here. The area would be much better suited to a combination of medical/professional offices and retail space. As such, when making your decision, we urgently implore that all of you involved please consider the well-being and wishes of the SunRiver residents.

Thank you, Mayor Randall, and to all others involved with the St. George City Council in the decision making of the proposed hotel at the Mohave Crossing development, for taking the time to review our concerns and strong opposition to the hotel, which will ultimately be detrimental to the SunRiver location. We trust that all of you will make the right decision to prioritize our community's safety and quality of life that we presently enjoy over any commercial interests that do not align with our residential location.

Thank you for your time.

Brent & Cindy Erickson

subject: Opposition to Building of Hotel in SunRiver (Mojave Crossing Project)
comment:
Dear Mayor Randall:

According to the Planning Commission's September 10th follow-up meeting and project-detailed changes resulting therefrom, we hereby submit this updated email in support of the email previously sent in June 2024 to Monica Smith, outlining our concerns and continued Strong Opposition to the building of a hotel that has no identifying brand ("Proposed Hotel") in the SunRiver Location ("SR Location"), and ask that it be added to our record and included in the decision-making process.

Building Site Adjustments (Hotel, Retail, Medical/Professional):

WE STRONGLY SUPPORT the part of the Mojave Crossing Development Project ("Mojave Project") that involves construction of the retail and medical/professional service businesses for the SR Location.

WE STRONGLY OPPOSE the part of the Mojave Project that involves construction of the Proposed Hotel for the SR Location to include, but not limited to, the following Community Safety Risks and Operations and Long-Term Concerns.
- Unlike other St. George hotels, the Proposed Hotel DOES NOT support a sufficient buffer zone (between residential and commercial properties) to ensure the safety and well-being of its nearby residents.
- Safety is often compromised when transient people are close to vulnerable elderly citizens.
- Hotels typically lead to increased crime. The proximity of the Proposed Hotel to SunRiver's 55+ Retirement Community would not only seriously jeopardize the safety and security of our community's elderly citizens, but also raise significant concerns about the overall safety of our community.
- The Proposed Hotel's 24-hour-daily operational hours and constant influx of guests will intensify the noise, light pollution, and increased traffic in the SR Location, all detrimental to elderly residents living nearby.
- The Mojave Project has not identified either the brand of the Proposed Hotel or the management team that would run it. This lack of transparency regarding the Proposed Hotel's ownership and management concerns all SunRiver residents.
- Excerpted from an NBC News report (12/25/2024) regarding residents in Kingston, NY: "Due to a surge in rents and home prices, many lower-income residents are being forced out of their homes and seeking shelter in hotels because it has become the only viable option for them to turn to for their living situation. This leads to subsidized and/or long-term housing, ultimately eroding the value of the community. The above situation is happening elsewhere as well."

As SunRiver residents we oppose any action which enables/promotes the erosion of our retirement community and compromises our safety.

St. George City's Buffer Zones: Although St. George City's revised plan regarding buffer zones meets the setback requirements according to its zoning laws and regulations, these zones are still insufficient to ensure the safety and well-being of nearby residents because of the Proposed Hotel's proximity to the SR Location.

Parking Concerns/Safety and Privacy Issues: St. George City's design for the Proposed Hotel parking is inadequate and DOES NOT accommodate for oversized vehicles such as RVs, trailers or larger trucks making narrow turns in its parking spaces. Additionally, the code requires the Proposed Hotel to have only two (2) employee parking spaces when similar hotels employ up to 30 employees during peak times. This shortage will certainly result in overflow parking on Sand Piper Drive, which borders residential backyards, thereby leading to safety and privacy concerns for its residents.

Trash Pickup: WE SUPPORT the Planning staff's recommendation that trash collection hours be scheduled between 8:00 a.m. and 6:00 p.m. ONLY, so that the area's residents can maintain the peaceful and tranquil enjoyment of their homes.

Sand Piper Drive - Right-Turn Exit Only: WE SUPPORT the Planning staff's request that ANY project surrounding Sand Piper Drive and Nighthawk Drive include a Right-Turn-Only Exit onto Nighthawk Drive. This requirement will reduce traffic volume and prevent delivery trucks from driving behind residential homes, which could ultimately lead to safety and privacy issues.

TO SUMMARIZE: SunRiver advocates for responsible development that aligns with St. George City's values. The St. George General Plan emphasizes the vision of SunRiver, a community where residents can walk, run, ride bikes, and drive their golf carts without fearing for their safety. This vision is not just a dream, but a shared value with which the entire community supports and aligns. The Mojave Project, on the other hand, DOES NOT support and DOES NOT align with this vision.

The SunRiver community recognizes that St. George's growth necessitates change, which also must factor in proper zoning as part of the change. The City Council's primary responsibility is to prioritize its residents' safety and well-being. While the SunRiver community supports development that benefits residents and developers, it should NEVER BE at the expense of community safety and well-being. We are advocates for responsible development, and we believe that this can be achieved without compromising our safety.

A safe community fosters trust and stability that supports St. George's local economy, property values, and a general high quality of life for all its residents. Zoning decisions that do not fully consider safety concerns can ultimately lead to long-term problems, especially for elderly and vulnerable residents. Neglecting safety in the Mojave Project could lead to such problems, which we must all strive to avoid.

FINAL REQUEST TO DENY HOTEL: As residents of SunRiver, we respectfully urge all of you involved with the Mojave Crossing Development Project to consider and prioritize the safety, integrity, and well-being of the SunRiver residents when making your decision to either approve or disapprove of the Proposed Hotel portion of the Mojave Project. Approving this portion would significantly compromise our community's safety. Therefore, we urge you to DENY only the Proposed Hotel portion of the Mojave Crossing Development Project for the SunRiver Location.

Thank you for taking the time to hear our concerns.

Bruce Barnes
Catherine Barnes
SunRiver Homeowners

- We request a right-turn only exit onto Nighthawk Drive to reduce traffic volume and prevent delivery trucks from driving behind residents homes.

We respectfully urge the City to prioritize the safety and integrity of our 55+ community by denying this project on the basis that it is incompatible with the adjoining community and conflicts with the Atkinville Interchange and SunRiver.

Sincerely,
Dan & Michaelene Rowe

subject: Public Comments Form
comment:
Dear Mayor & City Council Members,

We previously sent an email on December 28, 2024, regarding the Mojave Crossing Project. Thank you for responding, expressing your concerns as well, however, upon obtaining additional information through in-depth research, which has proven to be completely counter to the information we have been receiving from very few Sun River residents. We are writing to recant our earlier position and share our updated perspective on this matter. We have obtained a copy of the proposed plan changes for the hotel and believe the builder has gone above and beyond to satisfy the vision for "The District at SunRiver" plans as posted on our Sun River website.

Our Background

As we begin our 10th year as residents of Sun River, we reflect on the significant changes in our community and the surrounding area. The vision originally presented to us when we visited the Sun River sales office—a harmonious blend of natural beauty and development—has unfortunately not materialized as hoped. While we understood that development was inevitable, we did not anticipate the extent to which it would disrupt the characteristics of the area.

Our personal experience illustrates this: once enjoying a serene view of the sunrise over rolling mountains, we now face a towering rock wall topped with homes that overlook our windows (The Villas at Sun River). We also see the skyline interrupted by Top Golf poles and endure the bright red lights of the Hampton Inn sign, which exceed the original height and visual expectations.

While some additions, such as the office building for Physical Therapy and the Smith's grocery accessible by golf cart, have been positive, the broader impact of developments, including noise and visual intrusion, has been unexpected.

The Mojave Crossing hotel project may bring similar disruptions to residents along Sandpiper Drive, however, this is nothing new throughout the Sun River Development, as so many others can attest to.

Updated Concerns and Recommendations for your consideration

Buffer Zones and Setbacks
The revised plan appears to meets the city's setback requirements, it appears the new proposal for the hotel will provide the enhanced landscaping, sound barriers which will help mitigate the impact on nearby homes and preserve the well-being of the community.

Parking Deficiencies
Parking is a recurring issue with new developments. We propose designating the entire length of Sandpiper Drive a "no overnight parking zone." This measure would not only alleviate congestion but also ensure emergency vehicles have unobstructed access to all homes located in the area. According to the revised plan, the parking lot was changed to accommodate all businesses at all times.

Traffic and Foot Traffic Concerns
The proposed traffic exit onto Sandpiper Drive may be necessary, but an equally significant issue is the expected foot traffic into adjacent neighborhoods. Guests and their pets will naturally seek walking areas, potentially intruding into non-public residential spaces. Protective measures, such as designated walking paths, signage or barriers should be considered.

Trash Collection Hours
We strongly support planning staff's recommendation to restrict trash collection hours to between 8:00 a.m. and 6:00 p.m., consistent with previous projects. This regulation is essential for preserving residents' peace and quality of life.

Increased Crime
It has been suggested that a hotel in this area could lead to an increase in crime. This was an issue that was voiced time and again as the Hampton Inn was in the approval stage, we do not believe crime has increased in the Sun River area as a result of the Hampton Inn being located in our area (police statistics should be considered).

Changes made to the Hotel original plans
The Hotel has been changed from an extended stay hotel (which we believe this area was not zoned for) to a "High End" hotel which will attract different clientele, which we view as an attractive addition to this area.

Additional Suggestions

While we welcome thoughtful development, it should align with the community's character and needs. We encourage the incorporation of open spaces or even a city park to offset the impact of increased traffic and provide designated areas for outdoor activities and dog walking, reducing pressure on non-public neighborhood roads and parks.

Thank you for your attention to these concerns. We hope you will continue to prioritize the well-being of Sun River residents as you review this project. We look forward to your response and seeing the Mayor and City Council give careful consideration to the needs of our community.

Jeffrey & Vickie Edwards, SunRiver Residents

Honorable Mayor Randall and City Council Members:

While the members of Southern Utah Aviation Association (SUAA) appreciate the efforts of the City to develop a revised Non-Commercial Hanger Leasing Policy, there are concerns with the current draft document.

The immediate and primary concern is the lack of public comment time interval allowed by the City.

The FAA Policy Regarding Airport Rates and Charges (Federal Register Vol. 78, No. 175 pgs. 55330-55331) states:

1.1 The Department encourages direct resolution of differences at the local level between aeronautical users and the airport proprietor. Such resolution is best achieved through adequate and timely consultation between the airport proprietor and the aeronautical users about airport fees.

1.1.1 Airport proprietors should consult with aeronautical users well in advance, if practical, of introducing significant changes in charging systems and procedures or in the level of charges. The proprietor should provide adequate information to permit aeronautical users to evaluate the airport proprietor's justification for the change and to assess the reasonableness of the proposal. For consultations to be effective, airport proprietors should give due regard to the views of aeronautical users and to the effect upon them of changes in fees.

Publishing the draft Leasing Policy just days prior to the "public comment and vote" on the document does not constitute "well in advance". A typical public comment period is 30 to 90 days.

Brad Schuster, Northwest Mountain Region Manager for the Aircraft Owners & Pilots Association (AOPA), states that the City should allow time for our experts to review the document.

SUAA respectfully requests the Mayor and City Council table or postpone any vote on this issue to allow for a reasonable amount time (we request 90 days) for review and input from the aeronautical users.

A cursory review of the draft document has already generated the following concerns:

1. Paragraph 3.3, Not a Ground Lease. If a Lessee is leasing the ground upon which to build a hanger, how can this not be considered a "ground lease". This definition could restrict the lessee's ability to secure financing.

2. Paragraph 3.5, Termination. The final sentence that states "In the event of an immediate critical or safety-related Airport purpose. . . ". Does this mean the lease could be terminated immediately? This might be construed to be unlawful as Utah law requires termination clauses be clear and provide adequate notice. At a minimum, the statement referred to is unclear and needs to be defined—the way it's written suggests the City could terminate for any reason.

3. Paragraph 3.6.1. states the City would require a lessee to submit a copy of their airworthiness certificate? A quick AI search suggests it may not be legal for a city to request a copy of an airworthiness certificate. Also, the 2-year time frame may be realistic for some EAB kit planes, but totally inadequate for a scratch built EAB project. The final sentence says "a longer period as the City may agree", but doesn't define the process to do so. This section needs clarification.

4. Paragraph 3.6.2. States in part that "Based Aircraft must be flown at least once every six (6) months". This is a potential safety issue, and SUAA doesn't understand how the City can dictate how often a plane is flown. The FAA regulations on this should be researched.

5. Section 3.9 Subleasing and Assignments. This section is especially problematic and has generated significant feedback from our members.

a. Paragraph 3.9.2-Subleasing. This whole paragraph is untenable. This places an undue burden on small businesses that own blocks of hangers to rent out to airplane owners. This might even be challenged under fair business practices. Essentially we interpret it to mean the City wants 10% of the business's profits?!

b. Paragraph 3.9.3 Assignments. This also places an excessive burden on lessees. By law, fees must be reasonable and reflect actual costs incurred by the city (reference again the FAA document shown above). This would necessitate transparency by the City and potentially increase the accounting burden for the City. The paragraph also states that these fees be used for "asphalt improvements, taxi-way improvement and Airport construction". The "asphalt improvements" needs to be defined to show this would only be improvements at the airport. Any other use would be a violation of Federal law.

Once again, while the draft of the Leasing Policy is a good starting point, the draft document has not incorporated stakeholder input as required by the FAA for airports that receive Federal Funding. Working together to achieve a fair and equitable Leasing Agreement is not only in the best interest of all parties but will also satisfy the requirements under the FAA.

To reiterate, we respectfully request the Mayor and City Council table or postpone the vote on this Leasing Policy until these issues can be addressed.

Respectfully Submitted,

Jason Blake
Acting President
Southern Utah Aviation Association
782 So River Road, #64
St George, UT 84790

If you have questions or wish to discuss these points, I can be reached directly at my personal email [redacted-email]

subject: PUBLIC COMMENTS - Non-Commercial Airport Hangar Leasing policy
comment:
Dear Members of the St. George City Council,

I am writing to express my concerns regarding the proposed changes to the Non-Commercial Hangar Leasing Policy at the St. George Regional Airport. As a long-time leaseholder and investor with three hangars at the airport, I have made significant financial commitments totaling millions of dollars to support and enhance aviation infrastructure at SGU. While I appreciate the City's efforts to ensure equitable and efficient use of airport resources, I believe several provisions in the proposed policy will deeply negatively impact existing lessees and future investment in the airport.

1. Lease Term and Renewal Uncertainty

The proposed policy states that hangar leases for newly constructed facilities will have an initial term of 20 years with two possible five-year extensions, at the City's discretion. This creates uncertainty for long-term tenants who have made substantial financial commitments. The lack of guaranteed renewal terms makes it difficult to justify further investment in hangar development, as the return on investment is not assured. I urge the City to provide more defined renewal criteria and reasonable assurances for leaseholders in good standing.

2. Restriction on Leasehold Interest and Property Rights

The policy's assertion that all leases are not ground leases and that no lessee may record an interest in the property significantly limits leaseholders' ability to secure financing for hangar construction or improvement projects. This restriction places undue financial burden on private investors who rely on leasehold interests to secure funding for development. Allowing leaseholders to record their interests, with proper City oversight, would enhance financial security and encourage continued investment.

3. Lease Termination Provisions

The policy allows the City to terminate leases with a 90-day notice for non-urgent airport purposes or immediately for critical safety reasons. While ensuring airport safety is paramount, the broad discretion granted to the City creates instability for leaseholders. I recommend that lease termination provisions include reasonable protections for existing tenants, such as relocation assistance, extended notice periods, and full market, rather than "amortized", compensation for improvements made to the leased premises.

4. Limitations on Subleasing and Transfer Fees

The proposed policy severely limits hangar leasing and imposes a 10% fee on leases. Commercial lease profit margins run 8%-12%. This essentially eliminates any lease value in a hangar. Many private hangar owners rely on subleasing flexibility to offset costs. Restricting subleasing and imposing additional fees creates financial burdens for long-standing airport users. The pre-approval of a private property buyer puts the city in the middle of a private transaction. The 3% of assessed hangar value fee is not representative of the cost for the city to execute a lease transfer and allows the city to profit off the investment risk made by private citizens. I recommend the City reconsider these provisions to allow reasonable subleasing opportunities while ensuring compliance with airport regulations, as well as utilize a flat fee for lease transfers.

I appreciate the City's efforts to manage airport resources effectively, but I urge the Council to reconsider the above provisions which will impact long-term investment, financial stability, and fair treatment of existing leaseholders.

Thank you for your time and consideration.

Sincerely,

Josh Morales

www.zionairmotive.com

subject: OPPOSITION TO PROPOSED NON-COMMERCIAL AIRPORT HANGAR LEASING POLICY
comment:
Dear St. George City Council Members,

I am writing to formally oppose the adoption of the proposed Non-Commercial Airport Hangar Leasing Policy scheduled for consideration on March 6, 2025 (Agenda Item Number 05). As a concerned citizen and stakeholder, I believe the rushed process and substantive flaws in this policy not only deny adequate public input but also risk violating FAA Order 5190.6, the FAA Airport Compliance Manual, which governs federally obligated airports like St. George Regional Airport.

First and foremost, the timeline for public comment is insufficient. The agenda indicates this is a public hearing, yet the policy has only been reviewed in two City Council Work Meetings where airport tenants were barely allowed to comment. For a policy impacting hangar lessees, prospective applicants, and the broader aviation community, more time is essential to ensure meaningful feedback. FAA Order 5190.6, Chapter 3, emphasizes that airport sponsors must operate transparently and provide reasonable access to aeronautical facilities—rushing this adoption undermines that principle. I urge you to extend the comment period to align with both community needs and federal expectations.

The draft policy itself is troubling and appears out of step with FAA guidance. Section 3.2 states leases are "not a ground lease," despite lessees leasing the ground for hangar construction. This ambiguity could confuse property rights and financing, potentially conflicting with FAA Order 5190.6, Chapter 9, which requires clear, reasonable leasing terms to support aeronautical use. Adopting such unclear language is premature and risks legal disputes or noncompliance with federal grant assurances.

Equally troubling are the restrictive and costly terms. Sections 3.9.2 and 3.9.3 appear to permit subleasing of lessee-built hangars, yet Section 3.9.3 imposes a 3% transfer fee on the hangar's assessed value for assignments—framed as a fee but functioning like a tax. This charge, tied to property value rather than administrative costs, seems designed to generate revenue for airport improvements rather than recover processing expenses. FAA Order 5190.6, Chapter 4, requires fees to be reasonable and not unduly burdensome; this tax-like structure could discourage subleasing or sales, limiting access to aeronautical facilities and contradicting federal intent. Additionally, the stringent aeronautical use rules (Section 3.6, e.g., aircraft stored 14 days yearly and flown every six months), and the $8,000 wait list deposit (Section 5.2.1) compound these burdens.

I respectfully request that the City Council postpone adoption to allow a public comment period and a thorough revision for compliance with FAA Order 5190.6. The current draft risks violating federal obligations, overburdening lessees, and failing to serve the aviation community. Please reconsider this approach to ensure transparency, fairness, and alignment with both local and federal standards.

Thank you for your attention. I'm available to discuss this further and hope you'll prioritize community input and compliance before proceeding.

Sincerely,

Rex Donn

Pilot, Aircraft Manager, Flight Instructor, Hangar Builder, Aviation Enthusiast

subject: Comments regarding Hangar Lease Policy Changes at SGU Airport
comment:
Council,

Having read the City's proposed Non-Commercial Airport Hangar Leasing policy, I strongly urge the Council to table this abhorrent policy and instead engage with the airport community to develop more mutually-beneficial safeguards to public property and the aviation community.

General aviation plays a vital role in the community. Airports such as St. George avail thousands of non-airline passengers and their pilots an opportunity to visit southwestern Utah, providing millions of dollars of economic impact to the surrounding communities. In fact, an economic impact survey conducted through Utah State Aeronautics states that the airport's economic benefits far exceed the financial needs of the airport.

Predatorily pricing general aviation tenants out of hangar and land leases removes not only the community which sustains the airport's future, but comes at a detriment to the future aviation professionals who may have initially fueled their passions near their homes in St. George, only to find that the City swept these opportunities out from under them.

Mandating that aircraft be flown to justify leases among the requirements for home builders to accelerate the construction of their aircraft further puts unnecessary pressure on pilots that no municipality should have even considered imposing on general aviation. Pilots are under enough pressures internally and externally and no municipality should ever feel comfortable interjecting themselves into a pilots aeronautical decision making.

Lastly, these proposed changes come with no representation from current or future airport tenants, and it would be pretty naive to think that decisions like these should not come with the full support of those whose livelihoods will be threatened by such drastic changes. I propose that the City engage with local airport tenants and form an Airport Advisory Board that would leverage decades of expertise and experience in finding common sense, collaborative and cooperative solutions to problems that, through my own research, have yet to be identified, nor justified for such changes to be made.

As a founder of the Utah Aviation Coalition, the President of the Utah Back Country Pilots Association, a professional pilot for over 20 years, and a proud member of the general aviation community for over 35 years, I humbly ask the Council to immediately table these discussions and henceforth engage with the local general aviation community to help St. George continue to be an example of what's possible when a municipality seeks the collaborative and cooperative opportunities of the citizens they serve.

Roy Evans II
President, UBCP

Utah Back Country Pilots Association
Preserving and Protecting Utah's Back Country Airstrips Since 1996
utahbackcountrypilots.org

subject: Public Comment Hangar Leasing Policy
comment:
To Whom it May Concern,

I was made aware of the proposed changes to the City's Non-Commercial Airport Hangar Leasing Policy and would like to provide context and comments.

I propose that the new hangar leasing proposal be tabled at this time and reworked only if deemed necessary. If deemed necessary, all stakeholders should be part of the process and the ONLY goal should be to increase the hangar supply at SGU. As a ground lessee, and a hangar owner (read: stakeholder) I was not made aware of these changes which will directly affect my ability to use, maintain and someday sell my investment/hangar.

The stated reason for these proposed changes is: "Due to hangar demand..." No doubt, hangars are in high demand at SGU and there are many strategies to meet these demands. I would like to see the airport continue to grow in ALL aspects. Commercial service, maintenance facilities, FBO's and general aviation traffic will increase over the next few decades and we will need to be able to meet the demand. We will need to house more aircraft as the Greater Zion area continues to grow. I would like to see available hangar space keep up with demand.

The proposed changes to the leasing agreements will likely not meet that goal. I have found that any time regulations are tightened or operating costs increase, supply decreases follow. We need a different approach. I have the following concerns about the proposed rule changes:

1-The language of the proposed policy includes provisions for "city-owned" hangars. To the best of my knowledge, the city does not own any hangars. I cannot help but feel the proposed changes will pave a pathway for the city to acquire previously-built hangars by not renewing lease agreements. If the city plans on building hangars, so be it. Please do not plan on obtaining hangars by not renewing the land leases.

2-Many of these changes are not currently needed. There are no derelict hangars. I am also not aware of any tenants who are not paying. These changes won't increase hangar supply, and include changes outside of that scope. There must be a deeper reason.

3-Why is there a distinction between a lease and a ground lease? We lease the ground under our hangars. It used to be a very straightforward agreement that favored the city. Any further changes here will only convolute the agreements and therefore make it less-palatable to enter into new leases and build out more hangar space.

4-Leases should be a minimum of 20 years with renewal options lasting beyond the proposed 10 years. These hangars have to be viewed as an investment. If we can potentially lose all value after 30 years, this will be a barrier to building out new hangar spaces.

5- Speaking of renewals, I am concerned about language in 3.3 and 3.5. Section 3.3 states that if the hangar is in good repair that we will have the right to renew. "At the sole discretion of the city" is a challenging term. This needs to have defined criteria. Also, the city should not be able to offer or demand that a lessee enter into a new lease agreement at the will of the city.

6-Paragraph 3.5 states that upon termination (for any reason, in reality) the city will compensate the hangar owner. These values need to be well-established. This is very concerning language. See #1

These are just a sample of the concerns I see in the proposal. This proposal needs to be shelved.

Thank you for your consideration,

Ryan Bowler, DVM
Animal Clinic of St. George
[redacted-phone]

subject: URGENT: TABLE THE NON-COMMERCIAL HANGAR LEASING VOTE!
comment:
Dear St. George City Council Members,

I am writing to urgently request that you table the vote on the proposed Non-Commercial Airport Hangar Leasing Policy scheduled for this Thursday. This policy, which introduces a 1% sales fee and a $50/month sublease tax, fails to address the root issues at St. George Airport and instead imposes ongoing financial burdens on citizens and airport users. I strongly urge you to halt this vote and explore collaborative, practical alternatives that better serve our community and align with FAA guidelines.

The problems at the airport stem from mismanagement and a lack of hangar land improvements, not a policy deficit. To recap:

1. Mismanagement of Hangar Lease Land Demand: The previous airport manager was aware of growing hangar demand but failed to prioritize timely improvements to meet this need before it became critical.
2. Premature Lease Distribution: Leases were issued prematurely, leading to confusion and inefficiency in allocation.
3. Misplaced Blame and Lease Revocations: After revoking leases, the city has framed this as a "policy problem." The real issue is a lack of hangar lease land.

The proposed fees are intended to cover the shortfall in FAA funding, which only covers 35' of asphalt for the Group 2 taxiway. However, these fees amount to ongoing taxes that unfairly burden hangar owners and end users. Hangar owners are already paying for 15' of taxiway improvements on the front aprons of the buildings. Could we do something as simple as having the hangar owner asphalt or concrete 20'-30' to make up for the extra taxiway width that the FAA will not fund? In doing this, we could hopefully make this a one-time cost instead of the tax that the city is trying to implement with the 1% sales tax and $50/month sublease tax. This approach would reduce long-term costs for users and avoid potential conflicts with FAA guidelines, such as those in FAA Order 5190.6, which emphasize reasonable and non-discriminatory fees.

Alternative solutions exist to address the taxiway funding gap without resorting to ongoing taxes. For example, other airports have successfully leveraged federal grants, such as those from the FAA's Airport Improvement Program (AIP), which recently awarded $1.9 billion for infrastructure projects, including taxiway reconstructions. The city could explore additional AIP grants or state funding, as St. George did in 2023 when it secured $10 million from the Utah Legislature for airport projects, including a control tower. Additionally, establishing an airport commission or hosting public workshops, as suggested by other communities, could foster transparent dialogue and generate innovative funding ideas, such as public-private partnerships or phased development plans. These approaches could address the inventory shortage and taxiway needs while minimizing financial strain on users.

I know there are better solutions to this problem, but there must be someone willing to listen and work toward a reasonable outcome. While I appreciate Mr. Kemp's attendance at the Saturday morning breakfast, his dismissive attitude of "they are great guys, but we have a taxiway to pay for" does not foster collaboration or deliver the best possible outcome for end users. The policy's terms, such as the 1% transfer fee, may also conflict with FAA regulations, risking federal funding or legal challenges.

I urge the council to table this vote, extend the public comment period, and engage stakeholders in developing solutions like the proposed one-time taxiway contribution or grant-based funding. This will ensure the airport remains a vital regional asset without penalizing its users. Please confirm receipt of this letter and your consideration of these concerns.

Sincerely,

Rex Donn
Pilot, Aircraft Manager, Flight Instructor, Hangar builder, Aviation Enthusiast

subject: Water situation and building in St. George- Public comments
comment:
Dear Council Members,

My husband and I have lived here in St. George since 2002 with our family and loved the City and people, and working and serving in the community.

He taught at DSU (Tech) and started the Accounting program and Masters of Accounting, along with the Vita Program (free tax help with his students for 2,000 people in the community) for 10 years. He passed in 2017. I taught Kindergarten for 20 years with the District and taught 659 students in our District. I am retired, but continue to help with substituting in schools beside traveling the world!

We have seen much growth in the years we have lived here in St. George. However the past 10 years it has boomed literally.

I, along with many in our community, are very concerned with the continuation of growth and water situation for the needs of all building, moving in and expanding St. George and areas surrounding.

Questions of great concern:
1. What is the water situation?
2. Will we have enough water for all here with continued expansion and all the growth we have continued to have?
3. Are you concerned? Who is concerned? And what is the City council and St. George doing (actually have in place) to take care of future needs. It seems that much talk has been given about this and that and NOTHING done to solve the problem! Where will we get enough water for the community and all the people living here in the future 20 years and more.
4. What is the cap on building? Is there a cap? How many people are moving in as to compared to moving out? How many can live in this area to have enough water for all?
5. What is the City of St. George doing about water conservation (pools, lawns, water needs)? Is there going to be an allocation of water? If so, when and what? How can we conserve for our community?
6. Are many (including the council members) growing the community with no thought of their communities future water situation (only to expand their financial wealth and incomes)? What is happening? What cap do we need to take care of all here?
7. What are the plans for water? When is it to happen? Is it going to provide adequate water for all living here? Big questions for big problems?

Living in a desert is wonderful. Water is a big concern. When my husband and I moved in 20 years ago from 18 years in the southeast (lush green with many trees and lots of rain), we naturally knew that desert was dry (little water), we knew to landscape xeri scape (no lawn and plants indigenous to the area and no pool) because of desert water (very sparse). We knew to conserve. Our showers were always short and water turned off in sinks when washing, with short cycles on wash, and dishwasher.

St George is a playground of beauty. A desert playground with little water. Whoever lives here or speaks for the community, needs to live and know this, and do all in their power to continue to make this a place of beauty with water for all who live here. The water will run out if plans are not made to conserve and cap building.

Thank you for your time and help in these urgent matters.

Sincerely and hopeful,
Venna Barrett

A Recreation Preservation Commission would provide a voice for these resources.

It would work alongside developers and City leaders to find solutions that balance growth with protection—we can have both if we are thoughtful and responsible. The goal isn't to stop progress—it's to make sure we don't pave over the very things that make southern Utah such a wonderful place to live.

Because once these places are gone, they're gone for good. They cannot be replaced. Establishing a Recreation Preservation Commission ensures that the unique recreational assets of St. George are preserved—not just for us today, but for future generations who deserve to enjoy them too.

subject: Bike Park Construction
comment:
Dear Members of the St. George City Council,

I am writing to encourage the City to prioritize experience and proven expertise when selecting a contractor for the design and construction of bike parks and pump tracks. I am concerned that the parks department does not have a clear understanding of the importance of hiring experience and qualified contractors who specialize in these types of facilities. While it may be tempting to award these projects to the lowest bidder, facilities of this nature require a highly specialized skill set that directly impacts safety, longevity, and overall community value.

Bike parks and pump tracks are not typical site construction projects. They demand a deep understanding of rider flow, grading precision, drainage design, soil composition, and user safety across a wide range of skill levels. Contractors who specialize in this type of work have refined these elements through years of focused experience, resulting in facilities that are both functional and enduring. Firms such as Velosolutions have established international reputations by consistently delivering high-quality tracks that attract users, host events, and require less ongoing maintenance. St. George is already a member of the Sourcewell purchasing cooperative and could hire them without need for an RFP and get our very own, amazing bike park!

By contrast, an inexperienced contractor—even with strong general construction capabilities—may lack the nuanced knowledge required for these projects. Small errors in shaping, compaction, or drainage can lead to poor ride quality, accelerated deterioration, increased maintenance costs, and potential safety hazards. Worse, their poor design and execution means they simply don't get used. A good example of this is Santa Clara's skatepark which was built without any knowledge and experience and is unusable for bikes, skateboards, and scooters. While good intentioned, in many cases municipalities that initially chose a low-bid, inexperienced builder ultimately face costly repairs or full reconstruction, negating any upfront savings. This is evidenced by the need to pave the Snake Hollow pump tracks. It also appears that this will be the case for the new Curly Hollow bike pump track. Both contracts were awarded to the same, inexperienced contractor. My hope is that it won't be the case for the upcoming Lizard Wash or future bike parks.

Investing in an experienced contractor is not simply about quality—it is also about long-term fiscal responsibility. A properly designed and constructed bike park will last longer, perform better, and serve a broader segment of the community. It becomes an asset that supports recreation, tourism, and public health, rather than a liability requiring frequent fixes.

St. George has an opportunity to create a standout facility that reflects the City's commitment to quality and active living. A great example of this is Washington's newly opened Wheels Park which has already been celebrated and praised nation-wide. Selecting a contractor with a proven track record will help ensure that this investment delivers lasting value to residents and visitors alike. Choosing the inexperienced low-bidder is a waste of tax payer funds.

Thank you for your time and consideration.

Matt Metcalf, Architect
